# vc-x1-messages v0.3.3

Messages for the vc-x1 family. The open threads are the inbox, the history is the archive.

One shared repo every participant can reach is the only thing the protocol assumes. A thread is
one file, appended by everyone who takes part in it, so reading a conversation is reading one
file, and a search for a message's id returns everything ever said under it. Every member's
`custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.

## Terminology

Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
under it.

- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
  in any open thread.
- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
  eye, since the position already says it.
- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
  the close.
- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
  court until the answer comes.
- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
  Computed from the file alone.
- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
  thread naming the old id.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.

## Read Actions

### Read messages

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
   thread is the context to read it in.
2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.

### Find a thread

Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.

- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
  its bodies.
- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.

Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.

1. Take ownership.
2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).

### Fetch

1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
   working copy, and that is a write.

### Open a thread

1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
   file when it has one.

### Write a line

Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
the reply links the outcome by sha-link.

1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
   it has one.

### Close a thread

The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
and the close sits in the same commit.

1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.

## What is not here

- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
  cannot disagree with the threads.
- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
  and a reader takes what is there.
- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
  and that is the change it would take.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.
- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
  commit the rules require.
- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

## Versions

The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.

- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its

by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
the reply links the outcome by sha-link.

1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
   it has one.

### Close a thread

The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
and the close sits in the same commit.

1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.

## What is not here

- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
  cannot disagree with the threads.
- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
  and a reader takes what is there.
- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
  and that is the change it would take.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.
- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
  commit the rules require.
- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

## Versions

The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.

- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.

251-"Lines of context" to the longest file's length, or to a large number such as 1000 (`--context 1000`
252-is the CLI equivalent), to see the entire file, then select:

254-- **New version**: the file as it now is, with the added lines lit. This is what the permanent
255-  branch will carry, so it is the view for judging whether a change reads as one thing.

259-  which is the reading a reviewer wants when the edit is small and the file is not.

262-together changed the tree since a given `<base>` commit. To do that:

107:## vc-x1 push: what it does and does not do
108-
109-`vc-x1 push <bookmark> --yes --title "..." --body "..."` commits both repos with the approved title
110-and body (`--yes` because push's gates need a tty the agent sandbox lacks, and the user's approval
111-of the shown title and body already covers them), stamps each new commit's `ochid:` trailer
112-([above](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)), pushes the work bookmark, and squash-pushes the agent
113-repo's `main`. Three behaviors to keep in mind:
114-
115-- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 runs no build or tests. Validation is the per-rung
116-  flow's job, run *before* the push. The one check that remains is `push-work` verifying the
117-  bookmark's remote refs are tracked.
118-- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume: every stage no-ops when its work is
119-  already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If push exits after `push-work` but before
120-  the agent-repo publish, `vc-x1 squash-push -R <agent-dir>` by hand is the rest of it.
121-- **`ochid:` trailers are stamped by push** ([No hand-written
122-  trailers](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)), never hand-written into `--title` or `--body`.
123-- **The agent-repo is a linear journal.**
124-  - One push is one agent-repo commit on its `main`, paired with the work-repo commit, whatever
125-    bookmark the work-repo is on.
126-  - Never create an agent-repo bookmark mirroring a work-repo one: it steers session pushes at
127-    the wrong remote ref.
128-- **Squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a pass.
129-  - The agent keeps writing session data while the command runs, so its own record lands after
130-    the squash.
131-  - Session data is append-only, so a re-run never conflicts.
132-  - A single pass is never guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
133-
134-A late work-repo tweak after the push (a forgotten edit) needs `jj squash --ignore-immutable` and a
135-re-push, which is a remote rewrite and takes approval like any push.
136-
137-## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer
316-  commit made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a rebase onto the merge.
317-
318:## Local ladders
319-
320-The jj moves behind [Local ladders](../AGENTS.md#local-ladders), a rung's scratch chain of commits
321-that never leaves the machine. Ladder commits are scratch, for review and bisection only. Per ladder
322-commit:
323-
324-1. `jj new -R .`: a fresh empty `@`.
325-2. Do the commit's work.
326-3. `vc-x1 validate --fast` (the `[validate] fast` table). Non-negotiable.
327-4. `jj describe -m "..." -R .`: a scratch working title. This first-time authoring is the one
328-   permitted describe.
329-
330-At the end, squash the chain into the rung (below) and continue the per-rung flow from its
331-validation step. `vc-x1 push` then publishes the single commit and stamps its one `ochid:`. A
332-sub-cycle that deserves its own record nests the version suffix
333-([versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme)) and names its rungs like any other.
334-
335-Navigating:
336-
337-- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: the whole ladder from its base.
338-- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder commit by chid prefix, for bisection.
339-- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
340-- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in isolation.
341-
342-Modifying any ladder commit rewrites it in place, and descendants auto-rebase.
343-

## Trapezoid close-out recipe

The reshape behind the trapezoid shape, run at [Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) step 2: the
close-out commit, pushed linearly by the closing rung, becomes a merge whose first parent is the
trunk line and whose second parent is the cycle's ladder. Nothing here publishes, the merge goes out
with Land's fast-forward.

```
  main line   ...--<base>------------------<closeout>--
                      \                    /
  ladder             <rung-1>--...--<tip>-+
```

- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, the trunk position when the cycle opened. It
  becomes the first parent. Not always the previous close-out: a cycle landed linearly since
  (keep-separate shape, or a single-step cycle) sits on the trunk line and must stay there.
- `<tip>`: the cycle's last commit before the close-out. It becomes the second parent.
- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, reshaped here.

1. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`: `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent
   order is the argument order.
2. `jj new <closeout>`: an empty `@` above the merge. The bookmark followed the rewrite on its own.
   What step 1 leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r` re-parents descendants onto the
   rebased commit's old parent, so the empty `@` lands beside the merge on `<tip>` and the tree
   reverts to pre-close-out content, which looks alarming and is not.
3. Verify two parents: `jj log -r <closeout> -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
   both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>` is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at
   three consecutive close-outs), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from a correct one in
   `jj log --no-graph`.

Details:

- **Trailers survive.** The restore's squash and the reshape change `<closeout>`'s SHA but not its
  change id, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped at the closing push stay valid in both directions.
- **Immutability.** No flag is needed: a topic bookmark's commits are not on `trunk()` until Land's
  fast-forward.

Recovery:

- **Nothing is published until Land's fast-forward**, so the whole reshape is undoable with
  `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge**: undo and redo step 1 with the corrected revisions. Do not
  land a shape you did not intend. After the fast-forward the remote boundary is crossed and
  recovery is forward-only.
- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 2 skipped): `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Any
  commit made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a rebase onto the merge.

152:## Cycle bookmarks: create and land
153-
154-The mechanics behind [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section
155-holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
156-([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
157-
158-**Create**, at the cycle's opening, with the bookmark named by the cycle title's slug (the anchor
159-algorithm in [Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links), so the block's title heading
160-and the bookmark derive from one bare title):
161-
162-- `jj git push --named <bookmark>=@- -R .` is the common case: it creates the bookmark at the last
163-  committed change and publishes it in one invocation.
164-- Any other revision works as the `=<rev>` right-hand side. When `<rev>` is not `@-`, follow with
165-  `jj new <rev> -R .` so the working copy actually sits on the new line. Otherwise the bookmark
166-  exists and the next commit lands somewhere else.
167-- `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <rev> -R .` creates it without publishing, for a line that is not
168-  ready to be seen.
169-
170-**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent, begun by a
171-sync that found `main` unmoved ([Sync](../AGENTS.md#sync)). Every
172-`jj git push` in it is a push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push) and [Hard
173-stop after the final push](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push), its own approval, the
174-closing words before the final invocation, silence after ([At
175-rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)):
176-

178-   name](versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)): rename `<name>-dev` back to `<name>` in the manifest,
179-   `vc-x1 validate --fast` so the lockfile follows, and `jj squash` folds the edit into the closing
180-   (`@` sits directly above it).
181-2. Reshape per the recorded choice: trapezoid runs the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe),
182-   keep separate needs nothing. A single-step cycle has no choice recorded and its one commit lands

content.text:
No changes made; this is discussion only. Here's how I see the two tweaks fitting into **agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1**.

## 1. A review stop on a local commit before `vc-x1 push`

**What's there today.** The per-rung flow already has two stops: step 6 reviews the working-copy diff, and step 8 reviews the title and body. But neither shows you the commit itself, the description and the diff together as one object you can open in gitk. That object only exists once `vc-x1 push` creates it, and then it's already on the remote. So any fix after that is a remote rewrite (`jj squash --ignore-immutable` and a re-push) plus another agent-repo squash-push. That's what the last closing ran into.

**The tweak.** Step 8 becomes: write the description, then make a local commit (`jj commit` with the title and body). Then stop with "please review". You review it as a real commit: `jj show @-`, or gitk, since git's HEAD is that commit in a colocated repo. Fixes go into `@` and get `jj squash`ed into the local commit. Nothing on the remote changes, and nothing needs a squash-push. On your go, step 9 publishes it.

**The catch, in the code.** `vc-x1 push` with an empty `@` already publishes a hand-made commit as-is (`src/push.rs:567`, from bugs.md #4). But it doesn't stamp that commit's `ochid:` trailer. The agent-repo's trailer would point at the work commit, but nothing would point back. Two ways to close the gap:

- **Push learns to publish a local commit (my recommendation).** When `@` is empty and `@-` is an unpublished commit with no trailer, push adds the trailer to `@-`. That's allowed, since `@-` isn't published yet. It takes the agent-repo's title and body from that commit, so `--title`/`--body` aren't needed. The description is written once, in the commit, and reviewed there.
- **A recipe using only the rules.** Before pushing, run `jj edit @-` so the local commit becomes `@` again, then push it with the same title and body. That works today, but it's clumsy: the text has to match twice, and a mismatch silently replaces what you reviewed.

The first option is a vc-x1 code change, so one question is whether it runs as its own cycle first (something like "feat: push publishes a local commit") or as a code rung inside v0.3.1. I lean toward its own cycle, so v0.3.1 stays text-only and cites it.

**Related gap at Land.** The closing you review isn't what lands. Land restores the plain name by squashing into the closing, then reshapes the closing into the merge. Both are local until the final fast-forward push. The same idea would add a stop before that push, showing `git log --graph` of the reshaped trapezoid with the closing's final contents. Then what goes to `main` has been seen too.

## 2. Multi-step cycles always close as a trapezoid

**For it:**
- The trapezoid already keeps every rung reachable through the merge's second parent. So "keep separate" ("when the decomposition itself is informative") only adds a linear history. Plain `git log` still shows the rungs under a trapezoid.
- Recent practice already does it: the last three closings are trapezoids, including the dead-end one with only an opening.
- It removes a choice and a stop: Close-out step 5 (choose, record) goes away, and Land step 2 always runs the recipe.

**What it touches:**
- `AGENTS.md`: the rule-index entry "Shape at the first push", Cycle shape ("lands as a trapezoid or kept separate"), Close-out steps 5 to 7 (renumbered, and the "step 5 aside" reference in the intro), and Land step 6.
- `jj.md`: Close-out shapes shrinks to the trapezoid and the no-squash reason, and Land step 2.
- The mirrored headings in `rationale.md`.
- The `cycle-model.md` specimen's "Close-out shape:" line, which goes or becomes fixed text.

**Edge cases:**
- A ladder that shrinks to one rung still has an opening and a closing, so it's still a trapezoid, as the dead-end showed.
- Single-step cycles stay one linear commit.
- The dead-end item in v0.3.1 already says "lands as a trapezoid like any closing", so it gets simpler.
- One question: is there any case where you'd still want keep separate, or does "always" mean it's removed from the rules entirely and not kept as a user-only exception?

## Questions for you

1. Does the local-commit review replace step 8's description review, or come after it? My suggestion is that it replaces it, keeping step 6's diff review so you're not re-describing while the work is still moving.
2. Push stamping a local commit: its own cycle first, or a rung inside v0.3.1?
3. Do you want the review stop before Land's fast-forward too?
4. Is keep separate removed outright?

The plain version: today the only time you see the real commit is after it's already published, so fixing it means rewriting both repos' remotes. Making a local commit first and reviewing that keeps fixes local, but `vc-x1 push` needs a small change so the local commit still gets its cross-repo trailer. Making every multi-step cycle a trapezoid mostly deletes text and a decision point, and loses nothing, since the trapezoid already keeps every rung.

content.text:
I like it. It removes the rename from the cycle entirely, which also closes the Land gap I raised: the closing you review is what lands, apart from the trapezoid reshape. Some thoughts, mostly on the details.

**What goes away:**
- Opening step 6 (the rename), Land step 1 (restore the name, refresh the lockfile, squash it into the closing), and the `Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock` edits in every opening.
- The "dev rename always" item in v0.3.1. It gets replaced by "never rename".
- The rule becomes more general for adopters: "a mid-cycle build installs where consumers don't look". The Rust specifics live in each project's `[validate]`, not in the agent-files.

**`{version}` in the path: I'd use a constant root, `--root tmp/dev`:**
- The `[validate]` entries are literal invocations today. A `{version}` placeholder means `vc-x1 validate` has to read the version-of-record and substitute it. That's a new feature, and it's Rust-flavored unless the config also says where the version lives.
- A directory per version builds up one per rung. That's the litter `versioning.md` "Constant, not per-step" warns about, even though `tmp/` is gitignored.
- The version is already in the binary: `tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1 -V` reports the exact rung.
- Per-version directories only pay off if you want to run two rungs side by side. Is that something you want?

**`vc-x1 run-dev`:**
- With a constant root, `tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1 ...` works without a subcommand. `run-dev` would add finding the workspace root through `.vc-config.md`, so it works from any directory, and taking the path from config rather than hardcoding it. A key like `[dev] bin = "tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1"` would make it usable by other projects, not just vc-x1.
- It lives in the released binary, so it's usable from the cycle after it lands. That's fine.
- An alternative is no install at all: `cargo run --release --locked -- ...` runs the code under test. It costs a build check per call, though, and it isn't the same artifact `cargo install` produces.

**The catch: the build guard.** `build.rs:65` refuses a suffixed version under the name `vc-x1` on every cargo verb. It's what stops a mid-cycle `cargo install --path .` from replacing your stable `vc-x1` with unpushed code. Under this plan, a suffixed version has to build as `vc-x1` for `cargo test` and the `tmp/dev` install, so the guard as written must go. A build script can't see `--root`, so nothing simple replaces it. The options:
- Drop it, and accept that a bare `cargo install --path .` by hand mid-cycle replaces the stable binary. `validate` would never do that, so it would only be a human slip.
- Key it on the environment: refuse a suffixed release build unless `CARGO_INSTALL_ROOT` is set, and have `[validate]` set that variable instead of passing `--root`. Build scripts inherit cargo's environment, so the guard can see it. But it needs `validate` to support an environment on an entry, and a mid-cycle `cargo build --release` would also need the variable.

I lean toward dropping it. The risk only comes from a deliberate hand command, and Land's own `cargo install --path . --locked` happens at the bare version anyway.

**Where it goes:** it's a code change (`run-dev`, the guard, maybe `[dev]` in the schema) plus a rule change (Opening, Land, `versioning.md` Dev artifact name, and the rationale). Like the push change, I'd run the code as its own cycle before v0.3.1, or as a code rung in it. With two code changes now (push stamping a local commit, and this), one cycle "feat: ..." for both, or two, would leave v0.3.1 as text only.

The plain version: install mid-cycle builds into `tmp/dev` rather than renaming the package, and the rename and its undo at Land go away. Use one fixed directory, since the version is already inside the binary. The cost is the build-script guard that stops a dev build from replacing your real `vc-x1`. It can't tell where an install is going, so it either goes, or gets swapped for an environment-variable check.

message.content: An issue with using ./tmp/dev is it needs to be deleted each time otherwise it'll have stale information?

content.text:
I don't think it has to be deleted. Cargo's documentation says `cargo install --path` always builds and installs; it skips the "already installed and up to date" check that registry installs get. So each validate run overwrites `tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1`. What's left in `tmp/dev` after a run:

- `bin/vc-x1`: the binary from the last successful install. It's replaced every time.
- `.crates.toml` and `.crates2.json`: cargo's records of what's installed under that root. They're rewritten in place to the new version and source, not added to. They're how cargo knows the binary belongs to `vc-x1`, so overwriting it isn't a conflict.

Stale contents only happen two ways, and deleting the directory each time fixes neither:

- **A failed install.** If the build or clippy fails, `bin/vc-x1` is still the previous rung's binary. That's the same as `~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1-dev` today. `tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1 -V` shows which rung it is. `run-dev` could also check that against the version in `Cargo.toml` and refuse to run a mismatch, which is a stronger guard than deleting.
- **A binary that's removed or renamed in the package.** The old one might stay in `bin/`. I'm not sure whether cargo removes binaries that a reinstall of the same package no longer has. vc-x1 has one binary, so this doesn't come up here.

Per-version directories wouldn't fix this. They'd turn "one binary that might be a rung old" into "many binaries, most of them old".

I haven't tested this here. Two `validate --fast` runs at different versions, with `tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1 -V` and `cat tmp/dev/.crates2.json` after each, would confirm it. I'd make that a check in the rung that changes `[validate]`.

The plain version: cargo overwrites the binary and its bookkeeping files on every `--path` install, so nothing stale builds up. The one real risk is a failed build leaving the previous binary in place, and `run-dev` can catch that by comparing the binary's version with the source's.

3. Fast-forward: `jj bookmark set main -r <closeout> -R .`, then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
   This push publishes the reshaped commit, so the topic bookmark itself is never re-pushed.
4. Install: promote the artifact from `main`, the cycle's last act, run when nothing can enter the
   cycle anymore.
5. Delete the bookmark, locally and remotely: `jj bookmark delete <bookmark>`, then

   cycle](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)). The long-lived case below gets the same

An `[install]` table makes promotion work the same way. With the `--root` change:

- **`[validate] full` and `fast`** both end with `cargo install --path . --locked --root tmp/dev`. Every validation installs the dev build there, and nothing in a cycle touches the real `~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1`. That isn't a loss for full: today the closing's full run installs `vc-x1-dev` too, because the rename isn't undone until Land.
- **`[install]`** holds the promotion, `cargo install --path . --locked`, run only at Land step 4. As a key I'd write it `[install] release = ["cargo install --path . --locked"]`. It's a list, the same shape as `full` and `fast`, so a project whose install takes more than one step can say so.

**The guard moves into `vc-x1 install`.** A `vc-x1 install` subcommand that runs `[install] release` can check what `build.rs` can't: that `@-` is `main` and matches `main@origin`, `@` is empty, and the version is bare. The build.rs guard stopped a dev rung from replacing the stable binary. This does the same job where it can actually see the situation, so the build.rs guard goes. A hand-typed `cargo install --path .` stays unguarded, but the sanctioned way to install is guarded.

**`run-dev` needs the path.** The `tmp/dev` root would otherwise be written in both validate lines and again in `run-dev`. I'd add `[install] dev-bin = "tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1"`, so `run-dev` reads one key, and it could warn when `dev-bin -V` doesn't match `Cargo.toml`'s version, which is the stale-binary case. content.text:
Both fit, and together they close the last gap: what you review locally would be exactly what lands.

## The local commit is the trapezoid

If the subcommand (say `vc-x1 commit`) makes a multi-step cycle's closing as the merge itself, the reshape moves out of Land:

- **Shape:** the closing's first parent is `<base>`, the trunk position when the cycle opened. Its second parent is `<tip>`, the last rung. Rungs in between stay linear commits, and only the closing is a merge.
- **Finding `<base>`:** it's the fork point of the bookmark and `main`, the parent of the opening, so it doesn't need to be passed in.
- **Knowing it's the closing:** take an explicit flag (`--closing`) rather than guessing from the title. The " closing" and " dead-end closing" suffixes could be checked against the flag as a consistency test, not used as the trigger.
- **Tree:** `<base>` is an ancestor of `<tip>`, so the merge's tree is the same tree the closing would have had as a linear commit. Only the parents change.
- **What follows:** you review the merge with `git log --graph` or gitk, `vc-x1 push` publishes it on the bookmark, and Land is sync, fast-forward `main`, `vc-x1 install`, delete the bookmark. The trapezoid recipe, Land step 1, and Land step 2 all go. If `main` moved during the cycle, Land's sync already stops. The fix there is rebasing the ladder and the merge onto the new `main`, the same as today.
- **Single-step:** one linear commit, unchanged.

## The ochid is known up front

`vc-x1 push` commits the agent-repo's `@`. A jj commit keeps the change id of the change it commits, so the agent-repo commit's change id is `@`'s change id today. `vc-x1 commit` can therefore stamp `ochid: <prefix>/<agent @ chid>` into the local commit when it's made. The review shows the full description, trailer included, and push only checks it. Transcript writes during the review don't change that id, because jj snapshots keep the change id.

What can break it: anything that commits or abandons the agent-repo's `@` between the local commit and the push. Your `vc-x1 squash-push -R <agent-dir>` does that, and so does a stray `jj new` there. So push should compare the stamped id with the agent-repo's current `@` change id:

- If they match, publish as-is.
- If they don't, restamp the local commit. That's allowed because it isn't published yet. Then say so, since the description changed after review, even if only in the trailer line.

The other direction is the agent-repo commit's trailer, which points at the work commit. That id is fixed once the local commit exists.

## What this changes in the rules

- "Commit" changes meaning: `vc-x1 commit` makes the reviewable local commit, and `vc-x1 push` publishes it. The rule that no rung is pre-committed is replaced. Committing vs pushing, the per-rung flow's steps 8 and 9, and `jj.md`'s "vc-x1 push" section are rewritten around that.
- Push reads the title and body from the commit, so `--title` and `--body` go away for the work-repo. The description is written once, by `vc-x1 commit`.
- A late fix during review is `jj squash` into the local commit. For the closing, that's a squash into the merge. jj allows that, but it's worth a test.

The plain version: `vc-x1 commit` would make the closing as the trapezoid merge right away, and could fill in the agent-repo's trailer, because it can already tell what the agent-repo commit's id will be. You review the exact commit that lands, and Land is reduced to sync, fast-forward, install, and delete the bookmark. The one hazard is the agent-repo changing between commit and push. Push would detect that and fix the trailer before publishing.

7:## Prose form
8-
9-([why](rationale.md#prose-form))
10-
11-Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why* or
12-the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
13-[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
14-numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One fact
15-per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they
16-hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their
17-relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See [Semicolons](#semicolons) and [Typeable
18-punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
19-
20-Surfaces that use this shape:
21-
22-- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See [Doc
23-  comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
24-- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and agent-repo). The title is the commit-specific add-on.
25-  See [The per-rung flow](../AGENTS.md#the-per-rung-flow).
26-- The cycle-record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`. See [The In Progress
27-  block](notes.md#the-in-progress-block).
28-- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are
29-  still fine.
30-
31-Bullet *content* differs by surface:
32-
33-- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, arranged by
34-  [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
35-  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader meets
36-    first and it answers the problem
37-  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them is
38-    a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
39-  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A bullet
40-    wanting a paragraph belongs in the cycle-record instead
41-  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
42-    live in the cycle-record, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names, each
43-    reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs here
44-- **Cycle-record / todo**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what landed
45-  and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list. The diff
46-  is the mechanical record, the commit body the problem and solution, the cycle-record the design
47-  thinking, and none restates another.

(wink + agent, 2026-10-18, simplified and extended 2026-10-20) Small rule fixes learned by running
v0.3.0, dead-end cycles defined, and the end of every rung and of Land reshaped, so that what the
user reviews is what is published. Each item is the change, then why.

- Never rename: `[validate] full` and `fast` both install with
  `cargo install --path . --locked --root tmp/dev`, so a cycle never touches the consumers' binary
  and the package keeps its plain name throughout. Opening step 6 and Land step 1 go, and
  `versioning.md` Dev artifact name is rewritten around the root. Why: the rename's restore at Land
  changes the closing after its review, by a squash into a pushed commit.
  - Checked when it lands: two validate runs at different versions leave one
    `tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1`, its `-V` the second version, and `tmp/dev/.crates2.json` naming it.
  - Fast and full then differ only by `-- --include-ignored`, the fourteen `dr1_*` tests, and are
    identical once **dr-1 is built in Rust** drops their `#[ignore]`. What fast becomes is decided
    then.
- An `[install]` table: `release`, the promotion `vc-x1 install` runs at Land step 4,
  `["cargo install --path . --locked"]` here, and `dev-bin`, the dev install's binary,
  `"tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1"` here. `vc-x1 run-dev` runs `dev-bin` and warns when its `-V` is not the
  manifest's version, a failed install's stale binary. Why: Land step 4 names no command, and the
  `build.rs` name guard, which cannot see an install's root, moves into `vc-x1 install`, which
  checks that `@-` is `main` at `main@origin`, `@` is empty, and the version is bare.
  - Open: whether `vc-x1 install` refuses or warns when a check fails.
- A local commit before every push: per-rung flow step 8 becomes `vc-x1 commit`, which makes the
  rung a local commit with the written title and body, and the description review is of that
  commit, description and diff together, by `jj show @-` or gitk. A fix is a `jj squash` into it.
  Step 9's `vc-x1 push` publishes it, taking the agent-repo's title and body from the commit. Step
  6's work review stays ahead of it, so a description is not rewritten while the work still moves.
  Why: the last closing's review came after its push, so a change meant a remote rewrite and a
  squash-push in both repos.
  - Committing vs pushing is rewritten, `vc-x1 commit` committing and `vc-x1 push` publishing, and
    `jj.md`'s vc-x1 push section follows.
- The trailer known at commit time: `vc-x1 commit` stamps the work commit's `ochid:` with the
  agent-repo `@`'s change id, which the agent-repo commit keeps when push commits it. Push compares
  the two and, on a mismatch, restamps the unpublished commit and says so. Why: the reviewed
  description is then the published one, trailer included.
  - A mismatch comes from anything that commits or abandons the agent-repo's `@` between commit and
    push, `vc-x1 squash-push -R <agent-dir>` among them.
- The closing is the trapezoid: a multi-step cycle always closes as a trapezoid, and keep separate
  goes. `vc-x1 commit --closing` makes the closing as the merge itself, its first parent the fork
  point of the bookmark and `main`, its second the last rung, so the merge is what is reviewed and
  pushed, and Land is sync, fast-forward, install, and the bookmark's deletion. The trapezoid recipe
  and Close-out step 5 go, and `jj.md` Close-out shapes keeps the trapezoid and why squash is not a
  shape. Why: the trapezoid keeps every rung reachable, so keep separate adds only a linear log, and
  a reshape at Land is a change made after review.
  - The " closing" and " dead-end closing" title suffixes are checked against `--closing`, never
    its trigger.
  - Checked when it lands: a `jj squash` into the merge, the review-fix case, keeps both parents.
- Code first: all of the above but the rule text is code, the `[install]` keys, `vc-x1 commit`,
  `vc-x1 install`, `run-dev`, push's changes, and the guard's removal. The stale `vc-config.md`
  examples are fixed with the keys: fast's `["cargo test --bins"]`, full's `cargo test` without
  `-- --include-ignored`, and `test.fixtures`' `"../vc-x1-fixtures"` with its "skips with a notice"
  prose.
  - Open: one feat cycle ahead of this one, or rungs of it.
