content.content:
## How this file is read

The format is the config markdown carrier's own: the `toml` fences, concatenated in document
order, form the TOML that gets parsed. build.rs shares the filter (`src/md_fence.rs`) with the
instance-config loader, so the prototype and a `.vc-config.md` are read by one rule, and prose
outside the fences never reaches a parser.

The tag must be exactly `toml`. A fence tagged anything else, or tagged not at all, is prose like
the text around it and never reaches the parser, which is what lets one of these files show a
specimen config in a `text` fence without the specimen becoming configuration.

Shape: one TOML table per settable key, named by the key's path, dynamic segments quoted
(`[repo.category."<cat>"]`). Key order here is rendering order everywhere downstream. The
entries a key's table may carry:

- `homes`: which config file(s) may contain the key. vc-x1 writes it only into those files, and
  `vc-x1 config --validate` reports it as unknown anywhere else. The values:
  - `"user"`: the user-wide config, `~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml` (or
    `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/vc-x1/config.toml`). One per user, still TOML rather than markdown
  - `"workspace-code"`, `"workspace-agent"`: the work side's and the agent side's instance config
- `kind`: value shape, one of `"str"`, `"usize"`, `"bool"`, `"item-list"` (a comma-separated
  list in one string), `"str-list"` (a TOML array of strings, one element per item)
- `doc`: one-line description (rendered into generated configs, so keep it tight)
- `used-by`: what reads the value once it is set, which is a different question from `homes`:
  the command or flag it feeds, or the structural role it plays
- `default`: the built-in value, omitted when there is none
- `example`: representative value for keys with no default
- `required`: active (not commented) in generated configs. The value is role-specific, filled by
  `init`
- `reference`: optional override url for the key's docs. When absent (the norm) build.rs derives
  `<reference-base>/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#<anchor of the path>`, which is the key's own section
  below

## The prototype's own metadata

`[vc-config]` is this file's metadata rather than a settable key. `reference-base` is the bare
repo url every derived reference is built from: build.rs joins it with `/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#`
and the key's heading anchor, so a reference follows the repo's default branch and no branch name
is baked in. A fork points it at its own repo and edits its own copy of this file.

```toml
[vc-config]
reference-base = "https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1"
```

## How the keys resolve

The `agent-session.*` keys resolve git-style, most specific wins: CLI flag, then the workspace
instance config, then the user config (`~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml`), then the built-in default.

content.content:
- a configuration setting is a **config key**, e.g. `agent-session.col-width` (its TOML table and key
  joined by `.`), not a "path".
- a datum in a transcript's `--fields` inventory is a **field**, e.g. `message.content[].type`, its
  levels joined by `.`, with `[]` marking array elements.

## Build and install

A plain Rust crate: `cargo build`, `cargo test`, and

```
cargo install --path . --locked
```

installs one binary named by the manifest's `[package].name`. That name is deliberate, the
**single-name convention** (adopted 0.78.3, design record in
====
  disk, the holder being a background command ([The sandbox's placeholder
  files](notes/session-lock.md#the-sandboxs-placeholder-files)).

## Testing

The repo ships two flavors of tests:

- **Unit tests**: `#[cfg(test)] mod tests { ... }` blocks inside `src/*.rs`. These call
  library code directly (no subprocess spawn) and run fastest. The dual / POR fixture tests under
  `src/init.rs::tests` build throwaway workspaces by invoking `init::init` as a function.
- **CLI subprocess integration tests**: files under `tests/`. These spawn the `vc-x1` binary that
  Cargo built, and its absolute path lives in the `CARGO_BIN_EXE_vc-x1` env var that Cargo sets at
  compile time, which `env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_vc-x1")` reads and bakes into the test binary as a string
  literal. Argument parsing, exit codes, and stdout/stderr are all exercised end-to-end. Each
  subprocess gets a `HOME` override so the user's real `~/.config/vc-x1/` can't leak in or get
  clobbered.

Run everything with:

```bash
cargo test                 # unit + integration
cargo test --bins          # unit tests only, no binary spawned
cargo test --test cli_init # one integration test crate
```

### Acceptance fixtures

The lookup's tests run over pre-created dual workspaces with documented relationships, one per
name under the directory the work side's `[test] fixtures` key names, `../vc-x1-fixtures` here.
A test picks a fixture by name and skips with a notice when the path is absent, so `cargo test`
passes on a bare clone, and runs the fixture's cases when it is there.

- `dr-1`, `dr` for dual repo, is the simple one-to-one shape: a work repo and its agent repo at
  `.claude`, laid out as `vc-x1 clone` lays a dual workspace out, run through four cycles by

message.content: I think we should change all "commit" steps to be local just like our closing, that means every rung is the same. Thoughts only.

content.text:
I read "local just like our closing" as: every rung, the closing included, is made by one local `vc-x1 commit`, reviewed as a commit, and only then published, with nothing special about the closing beyond `--closing` giving it two parents. That's what the block already says, so no disagreement there. But taking "every rung is the same" seriously points at one thing in the plan that isn't uniform, and I think it should change:

**Today's plan is split across the two repos.** `vc-x1 commit` makes the work-repo commit, and the agent-repo commit is still made by `vc-x1 push`. That's why the plan has the trailer stamped from a *predicted* change id, with a mismatch check and a restamp at push. The split is the old flow surviving in half.

**The uniform version: `vc-x1 commit` commits both repos, locally, as a pair.** The work commit and the agent-repo commit are made together, each stamped with the other's change id, both known at that moment because both commits exist. Then `vc-x1 push` does nothing but publish: push the bookmark, push the agent-repo's `main`. What that changes:

- The trailer prediction, the mismatch check, and the restamp disappear. There's nothing to predict, and the "trailer known at commit time" item collapses into "commit makes the pair".
- `push` loses `--title` and `--body` entirely, in both repos. It carries no description, so a reviewed description can't be replaced on the way out.
- What you review with `jj show @-` in the work-repo is paired with an agent-repo commit that already exists, so `vc-x1 lookup` works on an unpushed rung too.
- One wrinkle: the review conversation itself. Today it lands in the rung's agent-repo commit because push makes that commit after the review. With commit first, the review's transcript is in the agent-repo's `@` when push runs. Push would squash it into the paired commit before publishing, which is allowed since that commit is unpublished, and a squash into `@-` keeps its change id, so the trailer stays right. That's the same move `squash-push` already makes, which also means your own `squash-push -R <agent-dir>` between commit and push does no harm: it publishes the pair's agent half early, and push finds it done.

**Pushing stays per rung.** Local commits make it *possible* to hold the whole ladder back and push once at Land, but I wouldn't: the remote is the backup, and approval per push is the rule. What changes is only that the push is a pure publish of something already reviewed.

**What this does to the ladder:** the rung `vc-x1 commit makes the rung's local commit` becomes "makes the rung's commit pair", and `push publishes the local commit` becomes "push only publishes". The trailer item in the v0.3.1 Todo entry and the block's Solution and Deliberation get rewritten when you say so, since the shape is fixed but the rungs ahead are still unpushed, so their titles can change.

The plain version: yes, make every rung the same, and go one step further than the plan: have `vc-x1 commit` make both repos' commits together, so push just publishes. That removes the guessing about the agent-repo's id entirely, and the only new move is push folding the review's transcript into the agent commit before it goes out.

message.content: I like that, but we must be able to continue working on that rung that means we need corresponding `squash` which does both repos?

lastPrompt: I like that, but we must be able to continue working on that rung that means we need corresponding `squash` which does both repos?

content.text:
Yes. Once a rung is a local pair, "continue working on it" means folding new work into that pair, and `jj squash` by hand would do one repo and know nothing about the other. So the set is three subcommands, each acting on both repos:

- **`vc-x1 commit`**: makes the pair from the two working copies, each stamped with the other's change id.
- **`vc-x1 squash`**: folds both working copies into the pair. The work-repo's `@`, the review fix, goes into the work commit, and the agent-repo's `@`, the review's transcript, into the agent commit. A squash keeps the destination's change id, so both trailers stay right without being touched.
- **`vc-x1 push`**: publishes the pair. Its first step is the agent-side half of squash, so the last of the review's transcript goes out with the rung, and it refuses when the work-repo's `@` isn't empty: that's unsquashed work, and the user says whether it's a `squash` or the next rung.

**What squash must check.** Only an unpublished commit may be rewritten, so squash refuses when the work commit is at or below `<bookmark>@origin`, and says that a fix to a pushed rung is a remote rewrite, which stays an explicit, approved act as it is today. The agent side can be published ahead of the work side, by your own `squash-push -R <agent-dir>` in between. Then squash folds only the work side and says so: that transcript goes with the next rung's commit, which is also where it would land today.

**Description changes.** A review that changes the title or body isn't a squash, it's a re-describe, and the rule says never `jj describe` a trailer-carrying commit. The pair carries trailers from the start, so the rule as written would forbid fixing a typo in an unpushed description. The way out is `squash --title/--body`, which rewrites both commits' descriptions and re-stamps the trailers itself, so the rule stays "never by hand" and gains "and never on a published commit", which is the part that matters. v0.3.1 would reword it.

**Where it lands in the plan.** The ladder gains a rung, `feat: vc-x1 squash folds work into the pair`, between commit and push, and the push rung shrinks to "push only publishes". The dead-end item isn't affected. When you say so I'll rewrite the block's Solution, Deliberation, and Ladder, and the trailer item in the v0.3.1 Todo entry, since those rungs are unpushed and can still be renamed.

The plain version: commit, squash, and push, each doing both repos. Squash is the "keep working on it" command, push refuses to publish over unsquashed work, and a description fix goes through squash too, so no one ever edits a trailer-carrying commit by hand.

I like it, with a few refinements. The thought behind it, as I read it: a write command never guesses which repo it acts on. `sync` today means "the repo I'm in" when given neither flag, which is fine for a read-mostly command, but a `commit` that silently acted on one repo of a dual workspace would make an unpaired commit, and `lookup` would find nothing. So the resolver for the four write commands:

- **`--scope`/`-s`** names the roles, `work`, `agent`, or `both`, in a dual workspace. `-R` with it names the workspace, by its root or either repo, and without `-R` the cwd finds it, as the read commands do today.
- **`--por`** says the target is a plain repo, no pair, and `-R` names it. No trailer, no partner, `jj commit` and `jj git push` with vc-x1's description discipline. The point of having it at all is one tool for both shapes.
- **Neither**: an error that says the two forms. Nothing defaults.

**The two mistakes become loud.** The flag is the user's statement and the command checks it against the directory: `--por` on a repo whose `.vc-config.md` names an agent-repo is an error, and `--scope` on a directory with no workspace config is one. That's cheap and catches the slip in both directions.

**Per command, what the scope means:**
- `commit`: `both` is the normal case, since the pair is the point. I'd make `-s work` and `-s agent` an error in a dual workspace: a half-commit there is an unpaired commit, which is exactly what the resolver exists to prevent. If someone really wants one, it's `--por -R <repo>`, said out loud.
- `squash`: `both` normally, a half for the real cases: `-s work` when the agent half was already published by your squash-push, `-s agent` when only the transcript moved.
- `push`: `both` normally, a half for a rerun after a partial failure, which push's doc already describes as the by-hand remainder.
- `squash-push`: with this design it *is* `push -s agent`, squash the transcript and publish `main`. I'd retire it into push, keeping `squash-push` as an alias for a while so your habit and the agent-files' text keep working.

**The bookmark argument.** Push takes `<bookmark>` today. With the pair already committed, the work bookmark is whatever `@-` sits on, so the positional can be inferred and kept as an optional check, "push refuses when `@-` isn't on the named bookmark". That removes one thing to type per push without removing the guard.

**One relaxation to consider:** `--por` alone meaning `-R .`. Your rule says `-R` is required with it, which keeps a POR write as explicit as a dual one. I'd keep your rule, since a cwd default is the guessing we're removing.

**Where it lands.** `options_flags` already has a `scope` parser and a `PorFlag` leaf, so a shared resolver for the write commands is one rung, ahead of commit, squash, and push, and the ladder becomes ten rungs. The agent-files' `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` becomes `vc-x1 push -s both` in v0.3.1, and `squash-push -R <agent-dir>` becomes `push -s agent`.

The plain version: every write command has to say which repos it acts on, `--scope` for a pair or `--por` for a lone repo, and errors otherwise. Commit only ever acts on the pair, squash and push can do one half when the halves are at different stages, and squash-push turns out to be push's agent half, so it folds into push.

content.text:
Good. That settles two things: `squash-push` stays, a command in its own right rather than an alias, and the scope short names make the daily command three characters shorter than today's path. Thoughts on each:

**`squash-push` and `push` are different answers to a non-empty `@`.** The two repos' working copies mean different things, which is what decides the split:
- The agent-repo's `@` is a journal. It's never empty while a session runs, and folding it is never a decision. So `push`'s agent half always folds `@` into the pair's agent commit before publishing, and `squash-push -s a` is that exact move alone, which is why it's your most-used command: it's the agent half of every push, run whenever you want the backup current.
- The work-repo's `@` is a decision. Unsquashed work there is either a fix to the rung or the start of the next one, and only the user knows which. So `push` refuses it, and `squash-push -s w` or `-s b` is the user saying "it's a fix, fold it and go", the no-questions form. The per-rung flow stays `commit`, `squash` when a review wants a fix, `push`, and squash-push is the user's shortcut, not the agent's.

**Short names.** `a`, `w`, `b`, with the long forms `agent`, `work`, `both` still accepted. The `work,agent` spelling that `sync` takes today would retire in favor of `b`. `sync` should take the same parser, so `vc-x1 sync --scope=both` in the agent-files becomes `sync -s b`, one resolver for the five commands. One thing to check at the resolver rung: that `-s` is free as a short flag on each of them.

**With the no-default rule**, `vc-x1 squash-push` alone is an error naming the two forms, and in a dual workspace the agent's push is `push -s b` and yours is `squash-push -s a`. For a POR, `squash-push --por -R <repo>` is a plain fold-and-push.

**On the ladder**, this changes nothing beyond what the resolver rung already carried: squash-push gets the resolver with the others, and the retirement I suggested is withdrawn.

The plain version: keep squash-push, give every write command and sync the same `-s a|w|b`, and let the two commands differ only in what they do with uncommitted work in the work-repo, where push asks and squash-push folds.

Agreed, and I'd take it all the way: `-s` is required on the five commands, no default, and the `--por -R` alternative goes. Reasons:

- **The write commands are already dual-only.** `push` and `squash-push` today find the agent-repo through the config and fail without one. `commit` and `squash` exist to make and maintain the pair. A POR has no pair, so a `commit --por` would be `jj commit` with a flag in front of it, and `jj` does that fine. `--por` stays where it is, on `clone`.
- **One rule is easier to state than two.** "Every write command and sync takes `-s a|w|b`, and errors without it" is the whole resolver. `-R` is then only ever the workspace, named by its root or either repo, and defaults to discovering it from the cwd, as the read commands do.
- **The error is the documentation.** `vc-x1 squash-push` alone prints the three scopes and what each means, so the no-default rule costs one line of help, not a second code path.

So the flow is `commit -s b`, `squash -s b` or a half, `push -s b`, and your `squash-push -s a`, with `sync -s b` at the sync points. The resolver rung gets smaller than I described, and the v0.3.1 text swaps `--scope=both` for `-s b` and `-R <agent-dir>` for `-s a`.

The plain version: `-s` is always typed, `--por` is only for clone, and the write commands stay what they already are, commands on the pair.

content.text:
That works, and it's cleaner than `--por` as a separate flag: `-s` then answers one question everywhere, "which repos", and `p` is the answer "this one, and it has no partner". Thoughts:

- **`-R` and `-s` split cleanly.** `-R` is where: the repo for `p`, the workspace, by its root or either repo, for `w`, `a`, `b`. `-s` is which. Both default the same way, the cwd for where, nothing for which.
- **The two-way check still holds.** `-s p` on a repo whose `.vc-config.md` makes it one side of a dual workspace is an error naming the side and the scope to use, since a plain commit there is the unpaired commit the resolver exists to prevent. `-s w|a|b` on a directory with no workspace config is the other error. A plain jj repo with no `.vc-config.md` at all is what `p` is for.
- **What `p` does per command.** `commit`: describe and commit, no trailer, the same description discipline. `squash`: fold `@` into `@-` when `@-` is unpublished. `push`: push the bookmark `@-` is on. `squash-push`: both. `sync`: what "neither flag" does today. So vc-x1's description and publishing discipline becomes usable on any repo, which is the value, while the pair-only parts, trailers and lookup, simply don't apply.
- **Clone and init.** Scope there means the layout made rather than touched: `b` makes a dual workspace, `p` a single repo, and `w` and `a` are errors since neither makes half a workspace. That's a small stretch of the word, and I think it reads fine, so `--por` retires from both and `PorFlag` goes.
- **One thing to check at the push rung:** the lookup's window matching recognizes push invocations in transcripts by their command text, and the fixture's recorded lines are `vc-x1 push <bookmark> ...`. Inserting `-s b` and dropping the bookmark mustn't break how a push is recognized, so that rung tests the new form against the old fixture lines.

The plain version: `-s p` makes the commands work on any single jj repo, `--por` goes away, and `-R` is only ever a path. The only places that need thought are clone and init, where the scope names the layout to create, and the lookup, which has to keep recognizing push lines in both the old and new form.

content.text:
Yes, as a rule I'd state it: **every command that touches a repo takes `-s`, required, and `-R` is optional everywhere, meaning where.** Thoughts on the edges:

- **Commands that touch no repo are exempt**, since the flag would mean nothing: `version`, `config`, `agent-session` on a transcript file, `validate-anchors`, `validate-todo`, `fix-todo`. The rule is "where a repo is involved", and that's most of the list.
- **Fixed-role commands still take it, as a check.** `validate` only ever runs the work side's table, and `validate-agent` only looks at the agent-repo. Typing `-s w` there is ceremony, but it keeps one rule instead of a list of exceptions, and `validate -s a` erroring with "the agent side has no validate table" teaches the model. I'd accept the ceremony for the uniformity. If it grates in practice, the exception list is a later, smaller change.
- **The four read commands already have `-s`**, `status`, `lookup`, `show`, `list`, as optional with a default. Making it required is the same change as for the writes, and `status` is the one where the default has real cost: a `status` reporting one repo while the other has unpushed work is a miss the acquaint check exists to catch.
- **`-R` is one thing everywhere:** a path into a workspace for `w`, `a`, `b`, resolved to its root from either repo, and the repo itself for `p`. Its default is the cwd. Today `squash-push` and `fix-desc` use `-R` to name the repo to act on, which is the role `-s` takes over.
- **Size.** This is now a sweep across about fifteen commands, their `tests/cli_*.rs` subprocess tests, the fixture's recorded command lines, and every `vc-x1 ...` invocation in the agent-files and README. I'd keep this cycle on its subject: the resolver rung defines the shared flag and applies it to what this cycle builds or changes, `commit`, `squash`, `push`, `squash-push`, and `sync`, and a Todo entry, "every repo command takes -s, required", sweeps the rest as its own cycle, where the read commands' defaults go and the docs are updated once. Otherwise this ladder grows past what the last cycle choked on.

The plain version: one rule, `-s` says which repos and is always typed where a repo is involved, `-R` says where and is always optional. This cycle applies it to the commands it's building, and a follow-up cycle applies it to the rest in one sweep.

content.content:
== validate

Run the workspace's configured validation commands.

Reads `[validate] full` (or `fast` with --fast) from the work
side's config and runs each element as one command, in order,
from the work repo root, printing each before it runs. The
first failure stops the run, naming the command and its exit
status, and the subcommand exits non-zero. An empty or missing
table is an error, not a pass. See `vc-x1 config work` for the
table's shape.

Usage: vc-x1 validate [OPTIONS]

== validate-agent

Check the agent repo is published (main matches main@origin).

At rest the agent repo's `main` always matches `main@origin`: the
bookmark only moves inside a push / squash-push run, which
publishes it in the same invocation. A mismatch means an earlier
publish was lost. Read-only and cheap (two jj lookups; no cargo
steps); also verifies main's remote refs are tracked. Exits
non-zero on any finding and fixes nothing: resolve with
`vc-x1 squash-push -R <bot-repo>`.

Usage: vc-x1 validate-agent [OPTIONS]

== validate-desc

Validate commit descriptions against the other repo.

Output columns: STATUS  CHANGEID  TITLE  [DETAILS]

Status labels:
  ok   : ochid trailer is valid
  err  : ochid has issues (wrong prefix, wrong length, ID not found)
  miss : no ochid trailer; shows match from other repo if found

Usage: vc-x1 validate-desc [OPTIONS] [REVISION] [COMMITS]

Arguments:
== validate-config

Check a workspace's config files.

Verifies every key is one the schema declares for that side,
the legacy schema is rejected, a dual workspace's two [repos]
registries agree, the file's own links resolve, and a side's
config carries `repos.work`. Read-only; exits non-zero when
anything is found. Was `config --validate` before 0.80.6.

Usage: vc-x1 validate-config [OPTIONS] [TARGET]

Arguments:
  [TARGET]
== validate-anchors

Check a markdown file's same-file links.

Verifies every `](#slug)` link and `[N]: #slug` definition
resolves to a heading in the same file, every `[[N]]` citation
has a definition and every definition is cited, and no two
headings slug to one anchor. Cross-file targets are skipped.
Read-only; exits non-zero when anything is found. With no
FILE, checks every `.md` in the workspace.

Usage: vc-x1 validate-anchors [OPTIONS] [FILE]...

Arguments:

I think that's right, and it makes `validate` mean one thing: run the scoped side's `[validate]` table. The pieces:

- **`validate -s w|a|b`** runs each scoped side's table. `validate.full` and `validate.fast` gain `workspace-agent` in their `homes`, so the agent-repo's `.vc-config.md` carries its own table, and `validate -s b` becomes the one command that validates a workspace. The agent side's table is its at-rest check, see the last point.
- **`validate-config -s w|a|b`** replaces its `TARGET` argument, which today is a path or a side name spelled its own way. The config's cross-side check, that the two `[repos]` registries agree, is what `b` runs.
- **`validate-desc -s w|a|b`**: the scope is whose commits are checked against the other repo, and `b` is both directions. Today it's one direction from the repo it's run in.
- **`validate-anchors`, `validate-todo`, `fix-todo`** take files, so `-s` names the tree the files are in, and with no file, the tree to sweep. `FILE` is then relative to the scoped repo's root, which is a small gain: `validate-todo -s w TODO.md` works from anywhere.
- **Dropping `validate-agent`.** Its check, `main` at `main@origin` with tracked refs, has two users: the subcommand and push's preflight, which call one function in `common.rs`. The function stays for push. The subcommand's job moves to `status`, where a verdict belongs: `status -s a` already prints clean or dirty, and the Todo entry **status prints a verdict per repo and exits with a bit per side** gives it the exit status a validate table needs. Then the agent side's table is `full = ["vc-x1 status -s a"]`, and `validate -s b` runs the work's commands and the agent's published check in one go, which also means every per-rung validation catches a lost publish, cheaply.
  - The order matters: `status`'s exit bit lands first, then `validate-agent` goes, so nothing is without a check in between. That's two rungs of the sweep cycle, not of this one.
- **The README's `validate-agent` section and the old-name rejection** in `main.rs` go with it, and the rejected pre-0.80.0 name's test too.

The plain version: every validate command takes `-s`, `validate` runs whatever table the scoped side has, the agent side's table is the published check, and `validate-agent` retires once `status` can exit non-zero, so `validate -s b` is the whole workspace in one command.

37	#### Solution
38	
39	Provisional, the Todo's plan as filed:
40	
41	- An `[install]` table in the config: `release`, the promotion,
42	  `["cargo install --path . --locked"]` here, `dev`, the dev install,
43	  `["cargo install --path . --locked --root tmp/dev"]` here, both lists like `[validate]`'s, and
44	  `dev-bin`, the dev install's binary, `"tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1"` here. `.vc-config.md`'s
45	  `[validate] full` ends with the dev install's line. The stale `vc-config.md` examples are fixed
46	  with the keys, fast's `["cargo test --bins"]`, full's `cargo test` without
47	  `-- --include-ignored`, and `test.fixtures`' `"../vc-x1-fixtures"` with its "skips with a notice"
48	  prose, and `vc-config-model.md` is regenerated.
49	- `vc-x1 commit` commits the work-repo's `@` with the given title and body and stamps its `ochid:`
50	  with the agent-repo `@`'s change id, which the agent-repo commit keeps when push commits it.
51	- `vc-x1 push` takes the title and body for the agent-repo commit from the work-repo's `@-`, so
52	  `--title` and `--body` go, compares the stamped `ochid:` with the agent-repo `@`'s change id,
53	  and on a mismatch restamps the unpublished commit and says so.
54	- `vc-x1 commit --closing` makes the commit as the trapezoid merge, its first parent the fork point
55	  of the bookmark and `main`, its second the last rung. The " closing" and " dead-end closing"
56	  title suffixes are checked against the flag, never its trigger.
57	- `vc-x1 install` runs `[install] release` after checking that `@-` is `main` at `main@origin`,
58	  `@` is empty, and the version is bare, and `vc-x1 install --dev` runs `[install] dev` with no
59	  check, the mid-cycle refresh of the dev binary.
60	- `vc-x1 run-dev` runs `[install] dev-bin` with the given arguments from any directory of the
61	  workspace, and warns when the binary's `-V` is not the manifest's version.
62	
63	#### Acceptance check
64	
65	In a scratch dual workspace made by the dev binary's `init`: `commit` makes a work-repo commit
66	whose `ochid:` names the agent-repo's `@`, and `push` publishes that commit unchanged, the
67	agent-repo commit's trailer naming it back. `commit --closing` on a bookmark of two rungs makes a
68	merge whose parents are the fork point and the second rung, and a `jj squash` into it keeps both.
69	`install` refuses, or warns, when `@-` is not `main` at `main@origin`, and `install --dev` leaves
70	`tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1` at the manifest's version. `run-dev -V` prints the manifest's version. In this
71	workspace, two full `validate` runs at different versions leave one binary under `tmp/dev`, its
72	`-V` the second version, and `tmp/dev/.crates2.json` naming it.
73	
74	#### Deliberation
75	
76	- Multi-step, eight rungs, a trapezoid the default, the agent's proposal and wink's go at the
77	  bookmark: opening, the install table, the local commit, push publishing it, the closing as the
78	  merge, install, run-dev, closing.
79	  - The install table is first, so every later rung's validation installs under `tmp/dev`.
80	  - The commit rungs come before install and run-dev, being the larger change, and the closing as
81	    the merge is its own rung, so the plain commit is reviewed before the merge builds on it.
82	- No rename, a bend of Opening step 6 and Land step 1, wink's say at the opening's review
83	  (2026-10-20): the cycle dogfoods its own change, so the opening keeps the name `vc-x1`, moves
84	  the two validate lines to `--root tmp/dev`, and removes the `build.rs` guard, which would refuse
85	  the suffixed version under the plain name on every cargo verb. The bend covers this cycle's
86	  pushes and its Land, which restores no name, and nothing else: the rule's text is v0.3.1's to
87	  change.
88	  - What the opening's validate run left behind before the bend, a `vc-x1-dev 0.85.6-0` in

  and on a mismatch restamps the unpublished commit and says so.

  of the bookmark and `main`, its second the last rung. The " closing" and " dead-end closing"
  title suffixes are checked against the flag, never its trigger.
- `vc-x1 install` runs `[install] release` after checking that `@-` is `main` at `main@origin`,
  `@` is empty, and the version is bare, and `vc-x1 install --dev` runs `[install] dev` with no
  check, the mid-cycle refresh of the dev binary.

  workspace, and warns when the binary's `-V` is not the manifest's version.

#### Acceptance check

In a scratch dual workspace made by the dev binary's `init`: `commit` makes a work-repo commit
whose `ochid:` names the agent-repo's `@`, and `push` publishes that commit unchanged, the

content.content:
inspected as-is (jj's operation log holds everything, so nothing is lost by stopping). Before
acting, sync captures each repo's pre-sync `jj op` id in memory, and the failure report lists
every repo's op id. The undo is explicit, per repo: `jj op restore <op> -R <repo>`. Nothing
persists across
invocations: a snapshot that outlives its run is a stale target waiting to rewind unrelated work.
That is also why the former `revert` subcommand was removed at 0.78.3: it restored the persisted
snapshot with no guard against discarding operations recorded after the failed sync. A safer
revert would derive its target from the op log and refuse when unrelated operations sit in
between. Until such a design exists, `jj op log` + `jj op restore` is the recovery.

```
vc-x1 sync                            # the repo in the current directory
vc-x1 sync --dry-run                  # look only: ask the remote, report, change nothing
vc-x1 sync --force                    # sync a repo sync would hold back, rebasing as needed
vc-x1 sync --scope=work               # only the work repo
vc-x1 sync --scope=agent              # only the agent repo
vc-x1 sync --scope=both               # both repos of a dual workspace
vc-x1 sync -R ../other                # sync ../other as a single repo
vc-x1 sync -R ../other --scope=work,bot   # ../other as workspace root
```

**Repo set resolution.** `-R` and `--scope` compose:

1. Neither: `.`, the one repo in the current directory, as `chid`, `desc`, `list`, and `show` take
   no flags. There is no walk up, so from a subdirectory of a repo `sync` fails with "There is no
   Jujutsu repo in ." and changes nothing.
2. `-R PATH` alone: sync just the repo at `PATH`.
3. `--scope=work|bot|work,bot` alone: workspace roles, resolved via the discovered workspace root's
   `.vc-config.md` (`work` -> root, `agent` -> the root-joined `agent` path).
4. `-R PATH --scope=ROLES`: roles resolved against `PATH` as the workspace root.

A named scope is cwd-portable: from the agent repo's directory, `vc-x1 sync --scope=both` walks up
to the workspace root and resolves both repos by absolute path. A bare `vc-x1 sync` there syncs the
agent repo alone.

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `-R, --repo <PATH>` | Workspace root, or a single repo to sync alone. Composes with `--scope` |
| `--scope <SCOPE>` | `work|bot|work,bot`: workspace roles to sync. Composes with `-R` |
| `-q, --quiet` | Suppress all output, exit code signals result (for scripts) |
| `--bookmark <NAME>` | Bookmark to sync in the work repo (bot repo always syncs `main`) [default: main] |
====
to do prints `<label>: clean` and exits 0 having touched nothing, so the command is safe to call
when you are unsure, and every other run prints that line again after the push. With work found it
acts without asking, which is what `squash-push.yes` defaults to, and `--ask` turns a confirmation
prompt on. The details of each are in the behavior notes below.

```
# In .claude: squash @ -> @-, advance main, push
vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude

# Bare invocation: same, in the current directory's repo
vc-x1 squash-push

# Name the bookmark explicitly, with a custom squash pair
vc-x1 squash-push feature -R . --squash @,@--

# Confirm before acting, overriding a configured squash-push.yes
vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude --ask
```

```
.claude: dirty: @ has changes. squash-push? [y/N] y
squash-push: squashing @ -> @-...
squash-push: setting bookmark 'main' to @-...
squash-push: pushing 'main' to origin...
squash-push: done
.claude: clean
```

```
# Nothing to do: no squash, no push, nothing touched
vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude
.claude: clean
```

Every at-rest run prints the verdict line before it acts as well as after, so a run that is about
to do something says what it found first:
====
vc-x1 init "$parent/work" --repo local="$parent"
work="$parent/work"
bot="$parent/work/.claude"

# 1. work repo: described commit -> advance main -> push
echo hello > "$work/hello.txt"
jj describe @ -R "$work" -m 'feat: add hello.txt'
jj bookmark set main -r @ -R "$work"
jj git push -R "$work"

# 2. bot repo: trailing writes -> squash-push (fold into @-, push)
echo notes > "$bot/notes.md"
vc-x1 squash-push -R "$bot"

# 3. cleanup when done (init also created a symlink under
#    ~/.claude/projects/ pointing at the fixture, remove it too)
rm -rf "$parent"
```

**Why `jj git push` for the work repo but `squash-push` for `.claude`?** The work repo's workflow is
a plain dev commit on `@-` that we push directly. The bot repo mirrors the bot's runtime pattern:
session writes land in `@` (above the last committed commit), and squash-push folds those trailing
writes into that commit just before pushing, so one atomic state goes upstream.

The run is synchronous, no background child, so what you see is the whole flow:
```
$ vc-x1 squash-push -R "$bot"
squash-push: squashing @ -> @-...
squash-push: setting bookmark 'main' to @-...
squash-push: pushing 'main' to origin...
squash-push: done
```

Preflight failures (bookmark missing, non-tracking remote, squash revset unresolved, conflicts, push
target lacks a description) exit with a non-zero status and a pointed error on stderr before
anything is rewritten.

### Testing the ochid-trailer guard

`squash-push` refuses to drop `ochid:` trailers: when the squash source's message carries trailers
the destination's message lacks, `--use-destination-message` would silently discard them and leave
the counterpart repo's cross-links dangling (the incident is recorded in [record finalize ochid-loss
bug (0.65.1)](./notes/chores/chores-13.md#docs-record-finalize-ochid-loss-bug-0651)). The guard runs
in preflight, before anything is rewritten.

`squash-push` always pushes, so the examples run against a throwaway init fixture (same shape as
[Testing push + squash-push](#testing-push--squash-push)) using its bot repo:

```bash
parent=$(mktemp -u /tmp/vc-x1-guard-XXXXXX)
vc-x1 init "$parent/work" --repo local="$parent"
bot="$parent/work/.claude"

# example 1, refusal: journal described on @ WITH an ochid
# trailer; squash-push exits 1 naming the trailer
echo b >> "$bot/notes.md"
jj describe -R "$bot" -m 'new journal

ochid: /abc123abc123'
vc-x1 squash-push -R "$bot"

# example 2, normal case: clear the description; the squash
# proceeds and the run pushes
jj describe -R "$bot" -m ''
vc-x1 squash-push -R "$bot"

# cleanup (also remove the fixture's ~/.claude/projects symlink)
rm -rf "$parent"
```

Output captured from a real run, and these transcripts are regenerated with
[`support/gen-exmpl-1-3.sh`](support/README.md#gen-example-1---3-output). Example 1 is refused with
exit 1:

```
$ vc-x1 squash-push -R "$bot"
error: refusing squash @ -> @-: the squash would drop ochid: trailers
the destination's message lacks:
  /abc123abc123
merge the messages by hand (`jj describe @- -R /tmp/vc-x1-guard-hmevVM/work/.claude`) or clear
the source's description, then retry
```

Example 2 with the description cleared squashes and pushes, exit 0:

```
$ vc-x1 squash-push -R "$bot"
squash-push: squashing @ -> @-...
squash-push: setting bookmark 'main' to @-...
squash-push: pushing 'main' to origin...
squash-push: done
```

vc-x1 sync                            # the repo in the current directory

vc-x1 sync --scope=agent              # only the agent repo
vc-x1 sync --scope=both               # both repos of a dual workspace

vc-x1 sync -R ../other --scope=work,bot   # ../other as workspace root
```

**Repo set resolution.** `-R` and `--scope` compose:

1. Neither: `.`, the one repo in the current directory, as `chid`, `desc`, `list`, and `show` take
   no flags. There is no walk up, so from a subdirectory of a repo `sync` fails with "There is no
   Jujutsu repo in ." and changes nothing.
2. `-R PATH` alone: sync just the repo at `PATH`.
3. `--scope=work|bot|work,bot` alone: workspace roles, resolved via the discovered workspace root's
   `.vc-config.md` (`work` -> root, `agent` -> the root-joined `agent` path).
4. `-R PATH --scope=ROLES`: roles resolved against `PATH` as the workspace root.

A named scope is cwd-portable: from the agent repo's directory, `vc-x1 sync --scope=both` walks up
to the workspace root and resolves both repos by absolute path. A bare `vc-x1 sync` there syncs the
agent repo alone.

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `-R, --repo <PATH>` | Workspace root, or a single repo to sync alone. Composes with `--scope` |
| `--scope <SCOPE>` | `work|bot|work,bot`: workspace roles to sync. Composes with `-R` |
''','''```
vc-x1 sync -s b                       # both repos of the dual workspace the cwd is in
vc-x1 sync -s b --dry-run             # look only: ask the remote, report, change nothing
vc-x1 sync -s b --force               # sync a repo sync would hold back, rebasing as needed
vc-x1 sync -s w                       # only the work repo
vc-x1 sync -s a                       # only the agent repo
vc-x1 sync -s p -R ../other           # ../other, a plain repo with no pair
vc-x1 sync -s b -R ../other           # the dual workspace ../other is in
```

**Repo set resolution.** `-s` says which repos and is required, `-R` says where and is optional,
the rule every write command follows, so a sync never guesses:

1. `-s w|a|b`: the sides of a dual workspace, resolved from the workspace `-R`, or the cwd, is in,
   by its root or either repo, through the root's `.vc-config.md` (`w` -> root, `a` -> the
   root-joined `agent` path, `b` -> both, work first). Outside a workspace it is an error naming
   `-s p`.
2. `-s p`: the repo `-R`, or the cwd, names, as itself. On either side of a dual workspace it is
   an error naming the side and its scope, since a plain operation on a side is half a workspace.
3. No `-s`: an error naming the four.

workspace root and resolves both repos by absolute path.

| `-R, --repo <PATH>` | Where: a path in the workspace, or the plain repo [default: the cwd] |
''')

message.content: How should this be done with v0.3.1 we're dogfooding?

content.text:
Under v0.3.1 this step is: `vc-x1 commit -s b` with the title and body makes the pair in both repos, the review is of the commit itself, `jj show @-` or gitk in each repo, a fix is edited and folded with `vc-x1 squash -s b`, and on your go `vc-x1 push -s b` publishes it untouched. The description I just showed you would be inside a commit, not in a chat message.

We can't run that yet: `commit`, `squash`, and the publish-only `push` are rungs 4 to 6 of this cycle, and the deliberation records that this cycle's own rungs go out by the installed `vc-x1 0.85.5` with `--title` and `--body`. What we can do now is the closest thing with what exists, and it costs nothing:

1. `jj describe @ -m "<title>\n\n<body>"`, so the working copy carries the description. That isn't the forbidden re-describe: `@` is unpublished and has no trailer, and it's the same first-time authoring a local ladder does.
2. You review `jj show @`, or `@` in gitk, description and diff as one object, with `tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1 validate-desc -s b` showing it as `miss` until push stamps it.
3. A fix is an edit in `@`, no squash needed, since `@` is the working copy.
4. `vc-x1 push --title --body` with the same text, which re-applies it and adds the trailer.

What it doesn't give is the agent-repo half of the pair, and the trailer in the reviewed text, which only `commit` can do. From the commit rung on, the dev binary has `commit -s b`, and whether this cycle's remaining rungs switch to `tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1 commit` and `push`, dogfooding the tool on the cycle that builds it, is your call to make then, recorded in the block like the rename bend was.

Shall I describe `@` with the title and body above, so you can review it as a commit before the push?

content.text:
Approved, so this rung goes out now, and the thoughts on the juggle come first, since nothing follows the push.

**On the order: commit, squash, squash-push.** I'd put `push` between commit and squash, so: commit, push, squash, then the stash. The reason is what today's `push` does when handed a pair. Its work half is fine: an empty `@` means it publishes `@-` as-is, the bugs.md #4 behavior, and `commit` has already stamped the trailer. Its agent half isn't: the agent `@` holds the journal, so push commits it as a *new* agent commit with `--title` and `--body`, on top of the pair's agent commit, both naming the same work commit. So the first rung made by `commit -s b` can't be published by the old push without that defect, and the push rung is what fixes it: fold the agent `@` into the pair's agent commit, refuse a non-empty work `@`, drop `--title`, `--body`, and the bookmark argument. It's a small rung, and with it in place every later rung can be dogfooded end to end, including squash's own rung, which is where the first "fix after review" will want it.

**The stash.** A2 carries both `sync` and `squash-push`, and I'd keep it whole as the rung after squash rather than split it again. Two things wait on it: a rebase onto the pushed rungs, `jj rebase -s wip-sync-squash-push -d <tip>`, and the one-word rename of `resolve_write_repos` in `squash_push.rs`, which the build will point at. It can sit on its bookmark until then.

**So the ladder would read:** opening, install table, validate-desc (this push), commit makes the pair, push only publishes the pair, squash folds work into the pair, sync and squash-push take -s, commit --closing makes the trapezoid, install, run-dev, closing. Same eleven rungs, two swapped relative to your vote. The block edit waits for your word.

Pushing now.

Yes, and I'd pull each piece out at the rung that gives it its second caller, which is the push rung for most of them, rather than now on one. What I see:

- **The description with its trailer.** `commit` builds `"{title}\n\n{body}\n\nochid: {prefix}{chid}"` twice, and push's `stage_commit_work` and `stage_commit_bot` build the same twice more. One `desc_helpers::with_trailer(title, body, prefix, chid)` is where the four meet, and where the trailing-newline trim belongs, so the push rung's extraction fixes the double blank line in both commands at once.
- **`--body @PATH`.** `body_text` is commit's today and push's at its rung. By the `options_flags` README it's a leaf, a `BodyOption` whose parser does the `@` read, flattened into both.
- **The scope resolved to a pair.** `Target::Pair { work, agent, .. }` with "both paths whatever the side" and "`-s a` alone is refused" is exactly what push and squash need: push to know which repo is which, squash to fold each side. A `common::resolve_pair(scope, repo)` returning the pair, with `Target` moved next to it, and `commit.rs` keeping only `agent_now`.
- **Snapshots and rollback.** Push has `Snapshots` and `rollback_on_failure` over both repos, commit has the same inline. One `Snapshots::take(work, agent)` and `restore`, which squash will want as well, since it rewrites two repos too.
- **The preflights.** "Refuse conflicts" and "refuse an empty `@`" are three lines each in commit and push, and squash-push's `preflight` has its own. Small enough that I'd only extract them if they grow a third copy.
- **"Does the agent `@-` name this work commit?"** The push rung's new case, and `squash`'s guard that a side is the pair's, so that's born shared: a `desc_helpers` check that reads the trailer and compares.

`common.rs` is over a thousand lines, so I'd rather the pair pieces went to a new `pair.rs`, with `common` keeping the resolver it already has, and the description pieces to `desc_helpers`, which already owns the trailer's shape.

vc-x1 push -s b                  # the pair, on the bookmark the work @- sits on
vc-x1 push -s b feature          # the same, the bookmark named as a check
vc-x1 push -s w                  # the work half only
vc-x1 push -s a                  # the agent half only, the remainder of a run that stopped
vc-x1 push -s p -R ../other      # a plain repo's @- on its bookmark, no trailer asked for
vc-x1 push -s b --dry-run        # plan and print, move nothing
```

What push refuses, with both repos as they were:

- a work `@` that is not empty: unsquashed work is a fix to fold or the next rung, the user's call
- a work `@-` with no `ochid:` trailer: not a pair's commit, so `commit` makes one first

| `commit-agent` | `jj commit` the journal as the partner, with the work commit's description and a trailer naming it, when the plan says so |
| `bookmark-set` | `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r @- -R .` and `jj bookmark set main -r @- -R <agent>` |
| `push-work` | Verify the bookmark's remote refs are tracked, then `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .` |
| `squash-push-agent` | Fold the journal into the partner and push `main` (see [squash-push](#squash-push)) |

reviewed. The transcript's push lines keep being recognized by the lookup in both the old form

* Push wrote descriptions and ran gates of its own.
  - The review gate, the message stage, the editor, `--title`, `--body`, and `--no-squash-push`
    are gone, and the retired flags are errors naming themselves. What remains is `-s`, `-R`, the
    bookmark as a check, `--dry-run`, and `--step` with `--yes` for its gates. A rerun stays safe,
    since every stage still checks its precondition.
* The pair can arrive in three states.
  - A `plan` stage reads them before anything is touched: the agent `@-` names the work commit
    (`commit -s b`) and the journal folds into it at squash-push, the agent `@` is the change the
    work commit names (`commit -s w`) and the journal is committed as the partner with the work
    commit's own text, or the agent repo changed since the commit and the unpublished work commit
    is restamped to name the agent `@`, said out loud, a published one refusing. Each state has a
    test, the restamp's keeping the work change id.
* The refusals had to come before any mutation.
  - Reading the agent `@` snapshots it, so a journal file the size limit refuses stops the plan
    with the file named and no rollback, the m-10-0 case now a CLI test of `commit -s b` for
    either side and of `push -s b` for the journal.

    remainder of a run that stopped past push-work, and `-s p` publishes a plain repo's `@-` on
    its bookmark with no trailer asked for. The bookmark is the line's unless named, and a name
    that is not among the nearest bookmarks below `@-` is refused naming them.
* The lookup knew push lines by two fixed prefixes.
  - It knows `commit` as a third verb, since the body now rides on it, and the binary by its
    basename after any path, since this cycle's rungs run `tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1`. The fixture's
    recorded lines still read as before.

  - The sync CLI test's peer push is `commit -s w` then `push -s w`, and `with_trailer` in

    **dr-1 is built in Rust** cycle's to retire, so a rebuild of the fixture after Land needs it

# Process-spawn ban, since 0.79.0. The mechanism, the ban as config,
# the grant as an attribute, this comment as the register, is
# explained in README.md under "No process spawns". A new
# `Command::new` site needs an entry below and a visible
# `#[allow(clippy::disallowed_methods)]` naming it.
#
# The register, closed (wink, 2026-08-19), reopened for entries 5
# and 6:
#
# 1. Version gate: the `jj -V` probe (src/version.rs). The gate
#    exists to compare the user's jj CLI against our jj-lib, so the
#    CLI spawn is its subject matter.
# 2. Push's `$EDITOR` launch (src/push.rs): interactive message
#    editing is a spawn by definition.
# 3. Init's gh provisioning (src/init.rs): `gh auth status`,
#    `gh repo view`, `gh repo create`. Creating a repo on GitHub is
#    the forge's REST API, not a version-control operation, and no jj or
#    git library can do it, and gh is GitHub's authenticated client.
# 4. Test helpers (src/test_helpers.rs and tests/common/mod.rs):
#    real-jj/git fixture setup and interop verification, kept
#    deliberately independent of the facade under test, and never a
#    substitute for asserting our jj-lib paths directly. The CLI
#    tests' launcher spawning the built vc-x1 binary is this entry
#    too: spawning the binary is what a CLI test is.
# 5. The validate subcommand (src/validate.rs): runs the
#    workspace's configured `[validate]` commands, which is its
#    whole job. Opened 2026-08-21 by the "empty custom-family into
#    the pinned set and config" cycle, whose plan put the checklist
#    commands in config for one subcommand to run.
# 6. Sync's remote look (src/jj/session.rs, `git_command`): two
#    git commands that ask a remote and move no ref. `git ls-remote
#    --heads <remote>` gives the commit each of the remote's
#    bookmarks is on, and `git fetch --refmap= --no-tags
#    --no-write-fetch-head` downloads the commits of the ones that
#    moved, so a fast-forward can be told from a rewrite before
#    anything is fetched. Sync has to know what a fetch would do
#    before it makes one, and a fetch changes the repo. jj-lib has no
#    such query: it spawns git itself for its network legs and keeps
#    that layer private, and it builds gix with no network client,
#    as of 0.45.1 and 0.46.0. Opened 2026-10-09 (wink) by the
#    "feat: sync is safe by default" cycle, and temporary: the entry
#    closes when jj-lib offers the query (TODO.md > ## Waiting).

# jj-lib's own git children (fetch/push/clone network legs, the
# default-branch query) are jj-lib's implementation detail, not
# vc-x1 spawn sites, and no lint here sees them.
#
# Environment-write ban, since 0.84.35 (bug 21 in notes/bugs.md).
# Tests run as threads of one process, so a write to its environment
# is seen by every test running beside it: `HOME` set to `/h` by one

**What the rung changed:**
- **`src/push.rs`, rewritten:** push carries no description. A `plan` stage reads the pair's state before anything is touched and refuses, with both repos as they were, a work `@` that isn't empty, a work `@-` with no trailer, or a named bookmark that isn't one of the line's. The agent half goes by what it finds: the agent `@-` names the work commit, so the journal folds into it; the agent `@` is the change the work commit names, so the journal is committed as the partner with the work commit's own text; or the agent repo changed since the commit, and the unpublished work commit is restamped to name the agent `@`, said out loud, a published one refusing. Then bookmark-set, push-work, squash-push-agent. `-s w`, `-s a`, and `-s p` are the halves and the plain repo. Gone: the review gate, the message stage, the `$EDITOR`, `--title`, `--body`, `--no-squash-push`, each retired flag an error naming itself.
- **Tests:** fourteen integration tests make pairs with `commit` and cover each plan state, the three refusals, the halves, the plain repo, dry run, rerun, rollback, and completion checks. The CLI size-limit test became three: `commit -s b` on either side, `push -s b` on the journal, and the required `-s`.
- **`desc_helpers::with_trailer`:** the one place a trailer is appended, used by commit and push, which fixes the double blank line.
- **The lookup:** `commit` is a third verb, and the binary is known by its basename after any path, so `tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1` lines count. Two tests.
- **Docs:** the README's push section and summary line, push's long help in `main.rs`, and the spawn register, where push's `$EDITOR` entry is closed in `clippy.toml`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, and the README.
- **`tests/cli_sync.rs`:** its peer push is `commit -s w` then `push -s w`. Note this file is also changed in the stash `wip-sync-squash-push`, so that rebase will conflict in it, which I'll resolve then.

**Dogfooded with `tmp/dev/bin/vc-x1`:** a bare `push` names `--scope`, `push -s b` on this workspace is refused with "unsquashed work", since this rung isn't committed yet, and `--title` is an unexpected argument.
